topic: Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: A student calculates that 8.0 g of copper sulfate crystals should form, but obtains 6.2 g after filtering, washing and drying. Which statement best explains the shortfall?
items.correct: Some of the product was left behind when it was separated from the mixture.
items.misconception: Some atoms were destroyed as the reaction took place, so less product formed.
items.why: Conservation of mass is learnt as a rule about a sealed flask, so when the balance reads short of the prediction students look for missing matter rather than for matter that is somewhere else. Ask where the atoms are, not whether they exist. Name the three places the specification allows: still unreacted in the mixture, left behind on the filter paper or glassware, or locked into a different product.
items.random_wrong: Mass is conserved only when the reaction is carried out in a sealed vessel.

items.q: An industrial reaction is written with a reversible arrow. Why does this reduce the yield of the product?
items.correct: The reaction does not go to completion, so reactants remain at the end.
items.misconception: The reaction runs backwards instead, so no product is obtained at all.
items.why: The double arrow is read as 'it goes backwards', and going backwards is pictured as a complete undoing rather than as a forward and a backward change happening in the same mixture. Read the arrow as 'both directions at once'. The mixture at the end contains product and reactant together, which is why the yield is reduced rather than zero.
items.random_wrong: The yield is fine if the mixture is simply left to run for much longer.

items.q: A student transfers a precipitate from the filter paper to a watch glass and some is left on the paper. What happens to the percentage yield?
items.correct: It falls, because the mass of product actually made is now smaller.
items.misconception: It rises, because the maximum theoretical mass used becomes smaller.
items.why: Division is remembered as 'big number first' from earlier arithmetic, and the equation is recalled as a pair of masses rather than as a fixed ratio of actual to theoretical. Anchor the equation to its meaning: the answer is the fraction of the possible product that was made, so the possible mass must be underneath.
items.random_wrong: It is unchanged, because no atoms can be lost in a chemical reaction.

items.q: Methane burned in a limited supply of air produces some carbon monoxide as well as carbon dioxide. Why is the yield of carbon dioxide lower than expected?
items.correct: Some of the reactants have reacted in a way different to the expected one.
items.misconception: Carbon atoms are lost from the system when carbon monoxide is formed.
items.why: The equation is treated as a complete description of what a mixture must do, so any other product is filed as an error or a loss rather than as a competing reaction with its own products. Treat every unexpected product as a second destination for the same atoms. Nothing is lost; the atoms are shared between two reactions, so the wanted one gets fewer.
items.random_wrong: The reaction is reversible, so carbon dioxide changes back into methane.

items.q: What does the percentage yield of a reaction compare?
items.correct: The mass of product actually made with the maximum theoretical mass.
items.misconception: The mass of the desired product with the total mass of all reactants.
items.why: Both are taught in the same section, both are percentages, and both are described loosely as being about 'how much product you get', which hides the fact that one is measured and one is calculated from the equation. Sort them by where the numbers come from: yield comes off a balance after an experiment, atom economy comes off the balanced equation before anyone does anything.
items.random_wrong: The maximum theoretical mass with the mass of product actually made.

items.q: The maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide is 8.0 g. A student obtains 6.4 g. What is the percentage yield?
items.why: Division is remembered as 'big number first' from earlier arithmetic, and the equation is recalled as a pair of masses rather than as a fixed ratio of actual to theoretical. Anchor the equation to its meaning: the answer is the fraction of the possible product that was made, so the possible mass must be underneath.

items.q: A preparation has a maximum theoretical mass of 3.6 g. After filtering, 2.7 g of dry product is collected. What is the percentage yield?
items.why: Division is remembered as 'big number first' from earlier arithmetic, and the equation is recalled as a pair of masses rather than as a fixed ratio of actual to theoretical. Anchor the equation to its meaning: the answer is the fraction of the possible product that was made, so the possible mass must be underneath.

items.q: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Relative formula masses: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide from 25 g of calcium carbonate?
items.why: Conservation of mass is remembered as 'mass in equals mass out' and then applied to one product rather than to all the products together. Conservation applies to the whole equation. Add every product, including any gas that escapes, and the total does match the reactants.

items.q: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Ar(Mg) = 24, Mr(MgO) = 40. What is the maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide from 4.8 g of magnesium?
items.why: The balancing numbers are applied one at a time instead of as a ratio, so the number in front of the product is used without checking the number in front of the reactant. Always write the ratio from both sides before converting: 2 mol Mg gives 2 mol MgO, which cancels to 1 : 1, so no doubling is involved.

items.q: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr(Fe2O3) = 160, Ar(Fe) = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of iron from 320 g of iron(III) oxide?
items.why: Balancing is practised as a puzzle about atom counts and then set aside, so the coefficients are seen as bookkeeping rather than as quantities that multiply the masses. Read 3CO aloud as 'three lots of CO'. If three lots go in, three lots of relative formula mass go into the sum.

items.q: What does the atom economy of a reaction measure?
items.correct: The amount of the starting materials that ends up as useful products.
items.misconception: The amount of the theoretical product that is obtained in practice.
items.why: Both are taught in the same section, both are percentages, and both are described loosely as being about 'how much product you get', which hides the fact that one is measured and one is calculated from the equation. Sort them by where the numbers come from: yield comes off a balance after an experiment, atom economy comes off the balanced equation before anyone does anything.
items.random_wrong: How carefully the product was separated from the reaction mixture.

items.q: Why is it important to use reactions with a high atom economy?
items.correct: Less starting material is wasted, which matters for cost and sustainability.
items.misconception: The percentage yield of the reaction is then certain to be high as well.
items.why: A 100% atom economy is read as a statement about what happened rather than about what the equation allows, so the ceiling is mistaken for the outcome. Atom economy says where the atoms could go if the reaction did exactly what the equation says. Yield says how much of that actually happened.
items.random_wrong: It shows that the product has been separated without any loss occurring.

items.q: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Relative formula masses: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. What is the atom economy for producing calcium oxide?
items.why: Atom economy is presented as a property of a reaction, like its rate, so the phrase 'desired product' in the equation is read as a label rather than as a choice that changes the answer. Name the desired product before starting the calculation, and quote the answer with that product named.

items.q: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr(Fe2O3) = 160, Mr(CO) = 28, Ar(Fe) = 56. What is the atom economy for producing iron?
items.why: Balancing is practised as a puzzle about atom counts and then set aside, so the coefficients are seen as bookkeeping rather than as quantities that multiply the masses. Read 3CO aloud as 'three lots of CO'. If three lots go in, three lots of relative formula mass go into the sum.

items.q: What goes on the bottom line of a percentage atom economy calculation?
items.correct: The relative formula masses of all the reactants shown in the equation.
items.misconception: The relative formula mass of the reactant containing the desired product.
items.why: Students trace the wanted atoms back to their source and stop there, because the other reactant feels like a helper rather than a starting material that also had to be bought. Every reactant is a starting material the process consumes. Atom economy measures the fraction of everything put in that comes out as the desired product.
items.random_wrong: The relative formula masses of the reactants without the balancing numbers.

items.q: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2. Ar(Zn) = 65, Mr(H2SO4) = 98, Mr(H2) = 2. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen?
items.why: Students trace the wanted atoms back to their source and stop there, because the other reactant feels like a helper rather than a starting material that also had to be bought. Every reactant is a starting material the process consumes. Atom economy measures the fraction of everything put in that comes out as the desired product.

items.q: Two pathways make the same product. Pathway 1: atom economy 100%, yield 95%, fast. Pathway 2: atom economy 55%, yield 95%, fast, by-product sold as fertiliser. Which choice is better justified?
items.correct: Pathway 1, because the same product is made from less starting material.
items.misconception: Pathway 2, because selling a by-product always outweighs a lower economy.
items.why: Atom economy is introduced alongside sustainable development, which gives it a moral weight that makes it feel like the deciding figure rather than one of several. Work through the data in the question one line at a time. A pathway is chosen on the whole set of figures the question supplies, and the specification names five of them.
items.random_wrong: Pathway 2, because a lower atom economy gives it the higher percentage yield.

items.q: Pathway A: atom economy 90%, reversible, reaches equilibrium at 12% yield, very slow. Pathway B: atom economy 60%, yield 90%, fast, by-product is useful. Why might B be chosen?
items.correct: B makes far more product per day and its by-product is still used.
items.misconception: A has to be chosen, because atom economy is the measure that decides.
items.why: Atom economy is introduced alongside sustainable development, which gives it a moral weight that makes it feel like the deciding figure rather than one of several. Work through the data in the question one line at a time. A pathway is chosen on the whole set of figures the question supplies, and the specification names five of them.
items.random_wrong: A is not possible at all, because a reversible reaction makes no product.

items.q: N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3 in a reversible reaction. Mr values: N2 = 28, H2 = 2, NH3 = 17. The atom economy is 100% but the percentage yield is low. Why?
items.correct: Every reactant atom can reach the ammonia, but the reaction is incomplete.
items.misconception: A 100% atom economy means the low percentage yield must be a measuring error.
items.why: A 100% atom economy is read as a statement about what happened rather than about what the equation allows, so the ceiling is mistaken for the outcome. Atom economy says where the atoms could go if the reaction did exactly what the equation says. Yield says how much of that actually happened.
items.random_wrong: Atom economy and percentage yield are the same, so one figure has to be wrong.

items.q: In which reaction is the atom economy for the named product 100%?
items.correct: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH, making ethanol
items.misconception: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, making calcium oxide
items.why: Atom economy is presented as a property of a reaction, like its rate, so the phrase 'desired product' in the equation is read as a label rather than as a choice that changes the answer. Name the desired product before starting the calculation, and quote the answer with that product named.

items.q: Crystals are left on the filter paper and stuck to the beaker. Has mass been destroyed?
items.correct: No. The crystals left behind still exist, they are just not on the balance. The actual yield falls and so does the percentage yield, but no atoms have been gained or lost.
items.misconception: Losing product when you filter or transfer it means mass has not been conserved, so the law of conservation of mass does not really hold in practicals.
items.why: Students meet conservation of mass and percentage yield in the same practical and merge them: any reading lower than expected is taken as evidence against the law rather than as product left in the apparatus. Separate the two ideas. Conservation of mass is about atoms in the reaction; percentage yield is about how much of the product reached the balance.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a percentage yield be greater than 100%?
items.correct: No. The maximum theoretical mass is the most that could possibly form, so the mass actually made cannot exceed it. A figure above 100% means the product was weighed before it was dry or pure, or the theoretical mass was calculated wrongly.
items.misconception: If you work really carefully you can get more product than the equation predicts, so a yield above 100% is just a very good result.
items.why: Percentage yield is treated as a score for practical skill, and scores can be beaten. The word 'maximum' in the equation is skimmed over. Point back at the word maximum. The theoretical mass assumes every atom goes where it is wanted and nothing is lost, so it is a ceiling that careful work approaches but cannot pass.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Would working more carefully and losing less product raise the atom economy?
items.correct: No. Atom economy is calculated from the balanced equation alone, so it is fixed for a given reaction. Working more carefully raises the percentage yield; only choosing a different reaction changes the atom economy.
items.misconception: Spilling less, filtering better and washing the crystals properly will push the atom economy up.
items.why: Atom economy is met straight after percentage yield, which really does depend on technique, so the same practical explanation is carried over to a quantity that never touches the laboratory. Ask what data the calculation needs. It needs only formulae and relative formula masses, so nothing that happens at the bench can appear in the answer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A reaction makes the desired product and a by-product the company sells. Should the by-product go on the top of the atom economy calculation?
items.correct: No. The top line is the relative formula mass of the desired product from the equation only. A saleable by-product may be a good reason to choose the reaction, but it does not change the atom economy for that product.
items.misconception: The by-product is useful too, so add its relative formula mass to the top of the calculation.
items.why: The definition is remembered as 'materials that end up as useful products', and a by-product that is sold obviously is useful, so it is swept into the numerator. Fix the desired product first, then apply the equation exactly. Report the usefulness of the by-product separately, as a reason for choosing the pathway.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Would leaving a reversible reaction running for much longer eventually give a 100% yield?
items.correct: No. A reversible reaction reaches a point where reactants and products are both present and the amounts stop changing, so waiting alone does not convert all the reactants.
items.misconception: A reversible reaction is really just a slow one, so give it enough time and every reactant will be converted.
items.why: Incomplete reaction is confused with slow reaction, because in most reactions students meet, waiting longer really does finish the job. Distinguish how fast from how far. A reversible reaction stops changing before all the reactants have been used, however long it is left.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: CaCO3 (Mr 100) -> CaO (Mr 56) + CO2. Does 25 g of calcium carbonate give 56 g of calcium oxide?
items.correct: No. The relative formula masses give the ratio, not the masses themselves. 25 g is a quarter of 100, so a quarter of 56 g forms, which is 14 g.
items.misconception: The relative formula masses in the equation are the masses in grams, so the answer is just the relative formula mass of the product.
items.why: The line '100 gives 56' is written down during teaching and remembered as a pair of masses rather than as a scaling factor to be applied to the mass in the question. Always scale. Write the equation masses underneath the formulae, then multiply both by the same factor to reach the mass given in the question.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.3.3 Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)
